en.title: Statement by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs at the High-level event entitled “From Island Heritage to World Heritage: Azerbaijan’s International Technical Assistance Initiative for Small Island Developing States”
en.description: Excellencies. Dear colleagues.
en.body:
Excellencies. Dear colleagues.

For an island nation, heritage is what tells future generations who we are, where we come from, and why our islands are home. It gives each generation the knowledge of its past, and with it, greater freedom to shape its future.

The Maldives therefore commends Azerbaijan for its proactive role as a member of UNESCO’s World Heritage Committee, and for translating that commitment into practical support for Small Island Developing States.

We need more countries and development partners to follow this path. SIDS require dedicated access to expertise, finance and capacity-building if we are to protect heritage that is both globally significant and uniquely vulnerable.

In the Maldives, protecting our heritage is a national priority under President Dr Muizzu.

Earlier this year, we submitted the nomination of the Coral Stone Mosque Ensembles of the Maldives for inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List. These mosques embody our Islamic heritage, our craftsmanship, and the ingenuity through which Maldivians adapted architecture to our island environment. We look forward with optimism to the evaluation process.

This nomination is part of a much broader effort to preserve our heritage.

We are strengthening the transmission of traditional crafts through new competency standards and training programmes. Dedicated training centres are being established for lacquer work, handicrafts and traditional mat weaving. We are also using modern technologies, including 3D scanning, to document our archaeological heritage and make this knowledge more accessible to researchers, students and the public.

But for SIDS, this work is becoming harder.

Climate change threatens historic structures, archaeological sites, traditional practices and community memory. When these are lost, they cannot simply be reconstructed.

That is why international cooperation must go beyond securing inscription on a list. It must help countries conserve, manage and transmit heritage afterwards.

We need greater access to conservation expertise.

We need stronger skills in documentation, restoration and site management.

We need climate-risk assessments and disaster preparedness tailored to heritage sites.

And we need to train a new generation of national heritage professionals.

This is precisely where initiatives such as Azerbaijan’s can make a difference. The Maldives looks forward to accessing the assistance offered through this initiative and to strengthening our own capacity to safeguard our heritage.

Our objective must be to ensure that climate change does not erase the history of nations that have contributed least to causing it.

Because safeguarding heritage is ultimately about ensuring that future generations inherit not only our islands, but the places, skills and stories that make them home, and the freedom to shape their own future.

I thank you.

en.title: Remarks by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs at the Annual Meeting of the United Nations General Assembly Platform for Women Leaders
en.description: Excellencies
en.body:
Excellencies

It is a particular pleasure to return to a platform that began during the Maldives’ presidency of the General Assembly, and that continues to bring women leaders together to place gender equality at the forefront of the multilateral arena.

For me, this conversation is personal. In 2009, I became the first Maldivian woman from the Foreign Service cadre to be appointed as an ambassador. Today, 17 years later, I have the honour of serving as the second woman Foreign Minister of the Maldives.

Those milestones taught me that presence is only the beginning. Women must have a voice that carries, a voice that shapes decisions, and the authority to lead.

Women’s leadership must reach beyond diplomacy and politics, into every island, village, and city, and that requires economic opportunity. For women entrepreneurs, access to finance is critical. In the Maldives, President Dr. Muizzu’s Government has announced a USD 6.5 million financing facility to support women entrepreneurs, with 25 per cent reserved for women with disabilities in our efforts to leave no one behind.

For women in SIDS, that opportunity matters. Affordable finance is already difficult to secure, and women entrepreneurs often face even greater constraints.

Voice also depends on visibility. When our data fails to capture women’s circumstances, their needs can disappear from the decisions governments make. Systemic barriers, financial inequity, and disproportionate climate impacts for women, all need to be measured in order to calculate the correct dosage of remedy required to level the playing field and empower women within society.

For SIDS, collecting detailed data across dispersed island populations is costly and difficult. Investment in national statistical capacity and digital data systems must therefore be part of our work on gender equality and the SDGs.

That commitment to making women’s voices count must also reach the UN itself.

The next Secretary-General of the UN should be a woman.

After eighty-one years, it is time for women’s leadership to reach the highest office of this Organisation.

That choice should carry no asterisk. A woman should be chosen for her ability, experience, integrity, and vision.

Women before us fought to be heard. Our generation must ensure that women’s voices shape decisions, and that women lead.

en.title: Statement by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs, at the High-level Meeting to Commemorate the Fortieth Anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development
en.description: President,
en.body:
President,

Forty years after the Declaration, the right to development has a clear meaning for the Maldives: every country should have the freedom and capacity to shape its own future.

The ambition of the Maldives is equally clear: President Dr Mohamed Muizzu has set the goal for the country to become a developed country by 2040. Achieving that goal requires sustained investment in our people, communities, infrastructure, and institutions.

For the Maldives, resilience begins with investment.

In practice, this means stronger schools and hospitals, adequate housing, reliable infrastructure, renewable energy, digital capacity, and new opportunities for our people. These investments will strengthen communities and give individuals greater security and opportunity, while increasing our national capacity to determine our own development path.

Yet, countries can only make these choices when they have the financial space to invest.

Development finance is becoming harder to access and increasingly expensive. High borrowing costs and debt repayments reduce the resources available for education, health, infrastructure, and other investments that directly improve people's lives.

This is where international cooperation matters.

Finance must become more accessible, adequate, and affordable. The Sevilla Commitment should be implemented, particularly its commitments on debt sustainability, concessional finance, and reform of the international financial architecture. Climate finance must become simpler and faster to access, especially for adaptation.

The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS gives us another part of the answer. Development cooperation should strengthen national institutions, expand domestic capacity, and support solutions determined by countries themselves.

Forty years ago, the Declaration recognized a right belonging to every person. Today, our responsibility is to create the conditions in which people and countries can exercise that right.

For the Maldives, that means having the space, capacity, and finance to invest in our own future.

That is how we build resilience. That is how we deliver development.

Thank you.

en.title: Remarks by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs at the High-level Event on Climate Action and the Just Transition
en.description: I would put it very simply. Three things must change.
en.body:
I would put it very simply. Three things must change.

First, we must close the gap between finance promised and finance delivered for adaptation.

Developed countries must meet their existing obligations and deliver the commitments already made through the COP process. There is no substitute for that.

Private, blended and innovative finance can add to public finance. They cannot replace it.

And for SIDS, finance must be predictable, accessible, and largely grant-based or highly concessional. Protecting people from climate change should not push countries deeper into debt.

Second, we need to move from financing projects to financing resilience.

In the Maldives, adaptation means:

- Protecting our islands and shorelines.
- Making critical infrastructure stronger.
- Protecting our coral reefs.
- Safeguarding communities and livelihoods.

That means resilience must be built into development itself.

And finance must reach countries faster. SIDS should not spend years navigating complex processes to access finance.

Third, we must judge adaptation by results on the ground.

Let us ask ourselves:

- Are communities safer?
- Is infrastructure stronger?
- Are livelihoods more secure?
- Are countries better able to withstand the next shock?

That should be the measure of success. Not simply how much was pledged, or how many projects were approved.

And one final point. Adaptation is not a substitute for mitigation. There are limits to what any island can adapt to. The more we delay cutting emissions, the harder and more costly adaptation becomes.

So, at COP31, let us move adaptation from planning to protection.

I thank you.

en.title: Remarks by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs at the commemoration of the Emirati Women’s Day 2026
en.description: Bismillahirahmaaniraheem
en.body:
Bismillahirahmaaniraheem

Her Excellency Heba Aljneibi, Head of Mission and Chargé d’Affaires of the Embassy of the United Arab Emirates in the Republic of Maldives, Dr. Mohamed Shauqee, Chancellor of Maldives National University, Dr. Aishath Shehenaz Adam, the Vice-Chancellor, Members of the Maldives National University, Excellencies, Distinguished guests, professors and our dear students, Assalaam Alaikum Warahmathullahi Wabarakaathu, and a very good morning to you all.

It is a great honour to join you in commemorating Emirati Women’s Day. On behalf of the Government and the people of the Maldives, I extend warm congratulations to the Government and the people of the United Arab Emirates, and especially to the Emirati women whose achievements we celebrate today.

I thank the Embassy of the UAE and the Maldives National University (MNU) for organising this event. A university is a fitting setting for this celebration. It is where knowledge builds confidence and the leaders of tomorrow begin to imagine what they can achieve.

This year marks the eleventh anniversary of Emirati Women’s Day, launched under the guidance of Her Highness Sheikha Fatima bint Mubarak, the “Mother of the Nation”. This year’s theme “We Emerge Stronger and Better” invites us to see every achievement should be the beginning of further progress.

To emerge stronger is to face challenges with courage and unity. To emerge better is to learn, adapt and create greater opportunities for the next generation. This theme therefore speaks not only to women’s advancement, but also about the advancement of society as a whole.

The experience of the UAE shows what can be achieved when women’s participation is central to nation-building. The late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan recognised that national progress required the full participation of women. Her Highness Sheikha Fatima bint Mubarak translated this vision into action helping create opportunities for Emirati women and strengthened their role in families, communities and national development.

Today, under the leadership of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the UAE, Emirati women continue to shape the country’s future. They are not simply part of the UAE’s success story, they are helping to write it. Let me share some remarkable statistics that I have come across that show the inclusion of Emirati women in nation-building – over 55 percent of Emirati Executive positions are held by women; in the Emirati private sector employment, 70 percent are women and 98 percent of them hold skilled positions. What is most defining about this initiative is its recognition of the achievements of women across Islamic nations. We are particularly proud that the Maldives marks 50 years of membership in the OIC this year.

Likewise, in the Maldives, under the leadership of His Excellency President Dr. Mohamed Muizzu, empowering women remains an important part of building a stronger, more inclusive and prosperous nation. I am proud to say that Maldivian women have always stood at the heart of our families, island communities and national institutions. Today they make important contributions across public service, parliamentary debates, education, healthcare, business, civil society and diplomacy. Women constitute the majority of the civil service and are strongly represented in the Foreign Service, where 91 women currently serve, including six serving ambassadors. Women also hold important leadership positions at the Maldives National University, while female students continue to feature prominently among the country’s highest academic achievers. Their contributions are equally significant in key economic sectors, including tourism, fisheries and agriculture. As the Maldives diversifies its economy, more women are becoming active in MSMEs, local tourism and other emerging industries, contributing meaningfully to national development. Their voices, talents, determination and resilience are shaping the nation’s progress.  Their growing role in decision making is more than a step toward equality, it is a powerful investment in the Maldives future.

As a woman entrusted with public office, I am proud to stand before you as one among many Maldivian women serving our country. My experience in diplomacy has shown me that we can make a difference in society.  The many senior women serving in the Maldives Foreign Service today have truly demonstrated the important contribution women can make through diplomacy. Inclusive decision-making enables institutions to benefit from a wider range of experience, talent and ideas.

However, our work is not complete. We must build systems in which every woman and girl has a fair opportunity to learn, lead and succeed.

To the students with us today, particularly the young women, believe in your ideas and in your ability to make a difference. Continue to learn, motivate each other and do not be discouraged when you face challenges. When you fall, you step up and rise even higher.

To the families, educators, institutions and colleagues I wish to emphasise that confidence grows where opportunity is real. Let us create environments in which women are heard, mentored and trusted with responsibility.

The Maldives looks forward to further strengthening its partnership with the UAE and remain deeply grateful for the UAE’s generous and continued assistance to the important development projects and social initiatives which have a had a meaningful impact on the lives of the Maldivian people. I also wish to convey my sincere gratitude to His Highness Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of UAE for the close and longstanding ties. between our two countries. I also thank Her Excellency Heba Aljneibi, Chargé d’Affaires and her team for organising this timely event and for bringing us together to celebrate this occasion.

Let me conclude by reaffirming a simple but important truth. Women’s empowerment is not a task for women alone; it is a shared national responsibility; and with women’s advancement comes shared prosperity and progress to all.

Thank you.

en.title: Remarks by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, at the Extraordinary Meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation
en.description: بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيْمِ
en.body:
بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيْمِ

His Highness Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,

Minister for Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Gambians Abroad of the Republic of The Gambia, His Excellency Sering Modou Njie,

Secretary General of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, His Excellency Hissein Brahim Taha,

Your Highnesses, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Assalamu Alaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakatuhu,

السَّلاَمُ عَلَيْكُمْ وَرَحْمَةُ اللهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ

The Maldives extends its warm congratulations to His Excellency Mr. Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed on his election as the Secretary- General of OIC. The election of a highly acclaimed statesman from the Islamic Republic of Mauritania speaks well the confidence placed on the country by the OIC Membership, in its invaluable role played to the cause of the Muslim Ummah.

We have no doubt that under his able leadership, the General Secretariat and the overall work of OIC would be further strengthened.

The Maldives wishes to pay a special tribute and its sincere gratitude to His Excellency Hissein Brahim Taha for his wise guidance and counsel in the work of the OIC during a critical phase of the Organization.

Excellencies,

For far too long, the subjugation of Palestine has gone unchecked.

For far too long, we have watched on,

As rights are denied, displacement continues and violence escalates.

The continued suffering of the Palestinian people demands more than expressions of concern. Our words must be translated into coordinated and meaningful action. To alleviate their constant suffering. To bring comfort to their enduring pain of displacement.

How many times must we gather here, in outrage and in sorrow, before we see our commitment translated into action?

It is a hopeful naivety that compels us to expect Israel to halt its genocidal acts in Palestine merely in response to condemnation.

An unjust and misplaced hope, one that has cost tens of thousands of Palestinian lives – men, women and innocent children - since the Nakba of 1948.

Despite our repeated calls for action, Israel continues to intensify its violations against the Palestinian people, targeting civilians and critical infrastructure including healthcare facilities, and restricting humanitarian efforts.

Your Highness, Excellencies and Distinguished Delegates,

Israel has now accelerated its settlement expansion and annexation of Palestinian land, deepening the occupation, driving further displacement and seeking to erase the very identity of the Palestinian people — in gross violation of international law.

The inaction of those who have vowed to protect humanity from such crimes is evidence of a collective moral failure.

Inaction is equivalent to complicity, and silence allows these atrocities to continue. This is why we cannot remain idle.

The Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict offers a critical pathway to peace, and the Maldives calls for its full and immediate implementation.

The Maldives strongly condemns the Israeli rejection of the Road Map for completing the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan, as endorsed by United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803.

We must ensure that commitments made through international efforts are not undermined. We must not allow this to become yet another unfulfilled promise.

Israel must be held accountable, by every means available to us.

The Maldives has stood with Palestine at every step and will continue to advocate for its rights in every forum.

We will not rest until an independent and sovereign State of Palestine is established on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital — a State in which the Palestinian people can live in peace, dignity and security.

As we gather here, we must reflect on the purpose that first brought us together, a shared commitment to safeguard our Ummah, and to help one another when we most need it.

The Maldives supports a stronger and more effective OIC that can advance real action for the Palestinian people.

We must aim for practical, results-oriented outcomes that are not only heard by the people of Palestine but also felt on the ground.

Excellencies,

For Palestine, the time for political rhetoric alone has passed.

Today I bring to this gathering, the commitment of my Government; the sentiments of every Maldivian; to raise our resolve to realise the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people.

Let us not leave Palestine with promises, let us leave with progress.

This will not be easy. But it is our collective responsibility; our moral responsibility to honour human rights; territorial integrity and sovereignty of the State of Palestine.

For it is Palestine today, but it may be any one of our own nations tomorrow.

I thank you.

en.title: Statement by Mr. Ahmed Shiaan, Secretary, Multilateral at the Closing Ceremony of the Small Island Developing States Global Business Network Forum 2026
en.description: Bismillah-ah-Rahman-ah-Raheem
en.body:
Bismillah-ah-Rahman-ah-Raheem

His Excellency Ngiraibelas Tmetuchl  Minister of Human Resources, Culture, Tourism and Development of Palau,

Mr. Hao Zhang, United Nations Resident Coordinator,

Distinguished Ambassadors and Permanent Representatives,

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

A very good afternoon to all!

Today, and yesterday, we have spent many hours – in this hall, and many others – discussing issues of utmost importance for small island developing States.

We have discussed how we can mobilize private-sector as a driver of action in the implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS.

We have looked at what needs to be done to create a space that enables finance to not just be available, but easily accessible, adequate and affordable.

We examined the role of artificial intelligence and digitalization in creating a SIDS economy that’s ready for a digital future.

We have also explored how tourism can become more resilient, in the face of growing risks, and how it can lead to stronger economies, and sustainable development that leaves no one behind.

These two days, we have also seen successes of this Forum since 2014. We’ve seen the opportunities for investment, for commerce, for development, in SIDS.

The task at hand now is to take these discussions and turn them into tangible action.

Use the networks we have built, the lessons we have learned, the expertise we have exchanged to make sure that we are able to provide a resilient prosperity for SIDS.

This Forum was the product of the hard work of many hands and many minds. And I wish to take a moment to thank them.

I thank our co-organizers the Government of Antigua and Barbuda, and the SIDS Centre of Excellence, as well as the United Nations Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States  for their excellent collaboration and cooperation to make this Forum and the launch of the Island Investment Forum a success.

I also wish to thank the Ministry of Economic Development, Transport, and Trade for their partnership with our team at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

I wish to also thank the Ministry of Finance and Public Enterprises, the Ministry of Climate Change, Environment and Energy, the Ministry of Fisheries, Agriculture, and Ocean Resources, and the Ministry of Tourism and Civil Aviation for their support to make this Forum, including tomorrow’s site visits a success!

I also wish to acknowledge with sincere appreciation the support we have received from the Maldives Transport and Contracting Company (MTCC), Maldives Industrial Fisheries Company (Mifco), State Electric Company (STELCO), Housing Development Corporation, and the Public Service Media (PSM) for ensuring this Forum has been an enjoyable and successful Forum!

I also recognize the excellent work by the event management team, ChopArt, and the support by Barceló Nasandhura Malé Hotel, to bring this Forum from the drawing boards to reality.

Maldives will remain open to all SIDS who are interested in learning more from our development journey. From our resilience building efforts. From our conservation stories.

The Maldives also remains open. For investment. For commerce. For enterprise.

When you go back to your homes, your islands, we hope that you recall your time here in the Maldives fondly. Our blue skies. Our turquoise waters. Our warm welcomes.

But most importantly, we hope you recall our biggest takeaway – development is destiny. But destiny is not mere fate. It is the consequence of the many choices we make; the many decisions we take; and the many hours we work.

I thank you.

en.title: Statement by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives at the Opening Ceremony of the Small Island Developing States Global Business Network Forum 2026
en.description: بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيْمِ
en.body:
بِسْمِ اللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيْمِ

His Excellency Dr Mohamed Muizzu, President of the Republic of Maldives,

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economic Development of Tuvalu, Honourable Panapasi Nelesone

Minister of Human Resources, Culture, Tourism & Development of Palau, Honourable Ngiraibelas Tmetuchl,

Minister of Economic Development, Transport and Trade His Excellency Mohamed Saeed,

Minister of Finance and Public Enterprises His Excellency Hassan Zareer

Cabinet Ministers and Senior Officials,

Ambassadors and Permanent Representatives,

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, a very good afternoon and “Maruhabaa” to the “sunny side of life”!

“SIDS can, and SIDS must lead!

We can shape and steer our future.

SIDS must stand as beacons of resilience and innovation.

Setting examples for the world to follow.”

Two years ago, in the “land of 365 beaches” – Antigua and Barbuda – President Dr Mohamed Muizzu, declared these words.

Words that began the journey that brings us all here today.

We are proud and happy to welcome you to the Maldives.

For a conference that will showcase our resilience and innovation.

That will build partnerships and friendships.

Prosperity and progress.

It was 37 years ago, on a sunny day like this, that representatives from small island developing States and their friends, from across the world, gathered in the Maldives, to discuss the impacts of sea level rise on small States.

On 18 November 1989, they adopted the Malé Declaration on Global Warming and Sea Level Rise.

That document became the catalyst for the creation of the Alliance of Small Island Developing States (AOSIS).

That conference became the first gathering of its kind.

The first time any State, small or large, had so publicly declared the destructive impact of global warming and sea level rise, as a threat to humanity.

Since then, small island developing States have become a driving force in global efforts to address climate change.

To ensure sustainable development, that leaves no one behind.

To mobilize affordable, adequate and accessible finance.

The Maldives is proud to have been a part of this story, alongside our fellow SIDS;

Together, we served in the trenches.

And dare I say, come out stronger.

We confronted the impossible challenges, with unparalleled determination.

We faced adversity, with hope.

The Maldives has been building on its legacy as an innovator - At home and abroad.

Under President Muizzu’s Maldives First foreign policy, we are determined to deepen our engagement on multilateral forums.

Have a seat at every table but also ensure we are heard.

Lead, especially on issues of critical importance for Maldives and others like us.

We are looking towards digitizing our economy, and artificial intelligence as the next phase of our development journey.

We are looking at generating our electricity through greener, more sustainable ways. And in turn, building more resilient and durable cities and islands.

We are looking at investing in a more creative people, building a more skilled, healthier, and educated workforce for the challenges of tomorrow.

We are investing in our digital infrastructure.

These plans, the lessons and challenges that shaped them, is what we hope to share with you here over these two days.

In 2014, the SIDS Global Business Network was launched to build connections, bridge divides, and boost investment.

A decade later, those connections span oceans and continents.

This network has been a vessel to find solutions for the very unique challenges the private sectors in our countries face.

It has also been a mechanism for investors to find partners in SIDS, generating projects and investments that continue to benefit our peoples.

Today, we go a step further.

Today, we will launch the Island Investment Forum – a key outcome from the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS (ABAS).

A vehicle that will find practical solutions, fund genuine partnerships, and direct much-needed finance, know-how, and investment into SIDS.

Sustainable development requires stronger partnerships with the private sector, investors and innovators.

Today, we bring together governments, business communities, private sector, academia and civil society.

It is the start of a renewed effort to invest in SIDS – especially in today’s very challenging global environment.

Our message – SIDS are not liabilities. We are good investments.

Our populations are young. They are educated and driven.

Our economies, small, yet robust and ready for innovation.

Here in the Maldives, we have many experiences to share. Many lessons we have learnt, and are ready to share.

Our pioneers have built the “World’s Leading Tourism Destination” from nothing.

Our fishing community have built the “most sustainable tuna fishery” from our traditions.

Today, we look ahead.

With the support of many partners within the Government, the State Owned Enterprises, and the private sector, we have put together a programme that will combine discussions on challenges, best practices, and practical solutions.

We hope our efforts will result in a productive, and useful stay here in the Maldives.

The Maldives is preparing for an ambitious future. A developed country by 2040.

But we know we cannot do it alone.

We believe in partnerships. Efforts that “raise all boats”.

Because this winding path of development, is fraught with ups and downs, surprises and hardships.

It is a path, best travelled, with friends by your side – supporting you through the pain, and celebrating with you through the wins.

I wish to express our sincere appreciation to his Excellency the President for granting us with his presence at this event today.

Before I conclude, I wish to express my sincere appreciation to the Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States (UN-OHRLLS), as well as the United Nations Resident Coordinators’ Offices, for their continued support and valuable contributions.

I also wish to extend my sincere appreciation to the Minister of Economic Development, Transport and Trade His Excellency Mohamed Saeed, and his dedicated team, especially Invest Maldives, for partnering with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in delivering this Forum.

I also wish to extend my thanks to the Ministry of Finance and Public Enterprise His Excellency Hassan Zareer especially the Planning Department for the support extended in organising the field visits.

Once again, welcome to the Maldives. Where the sun, seas and sand are 24/7, (except ofcourse when it rains).

We hope you enjoy our vivid blues, our bright turquoises, and exceptional whites.

But most importantly, we hope that this opportunity provides the space to build strong networks, learn new solutions and foster new partnerships that will bring resilient prosperity for our countries, our peoples; for generations to come.

I thank you.

en.title: Remarks by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, at the Diplomatic Outreach Event
en.description: Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,
en.body:
Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Assalam alaikum and a very good evening.

Tomorrow is our 61st anniversary of independence. Certainly, a joyous occasion for any nation.

Made even more special with your presence here with us.

A heartfelt welcome to all of you here today.

I wish to acknowledge the presence of His Excellency Dr Khalilur Rahman, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, Special Guest of the Government of Maldives to participate in the events marking the 61st Independence Day.

Thank you, my dear colleague, for being here.

The Minister has also been elected as the President of the General Assembly. I congratulate him on this achievement and wish him the best.

I wish to also acknowledge the presence of my fellow cabinet colleagues:

The Minister of Economic Development, Transport, and Trade, His Excellency Mohamed Saeed

The Minister of Fisheries, Agriculture, and Ocean Resources, His Excellency Ahmed Shiyam

And the Minister of Climate Change, Environment, and Energy His Excellency Ali Shareef

Welcome to all.

For much of history, nations have been measured by what they own.

The size of their territories.

The strength in their economies.

The resources they command.

And, the power they are able to project.

Imagine, for a moment, the Maldives in 1965.  A newly independent nation taking its first steps into the international community.

No vast territory. No large economy. No abundance of resources. No hard power to project beyond our shores.

By conventional measures, this did not look like a country that would survive – let alone succeed.

There was little to indicate the journey that lay ahead.

But what we had was our independence.

Independence gave us the freedom to shape our future, the freedom to pursue our foreign policy, and the freedom to define our own path.

But from the very start, we knew that independence alone would not be enough.

It was the friendships we forged, the partnerships we built, and the trust we earned among nations that gave us the strength to walk that path.

The story of the Maldives was never written alone.

It was shaped by the many countries and the many partners who stood with us as we found our place in the world.

Many of the nations represented here tonight have been part of that journey.

You supported our aspirations. Invested in our people. And, opened doors for cooperation to better engage with the world.

For that friendship, and for that trust, we remain deeply grateful.

Over the past six decades, the Maldives has transformed in ways that few could have foreseen.

We have built a world-renowned tourism sector.

We have led the way in sustainable fisheries.

We have expanded our international partnerships.

We have become a committed voice on issues including climate change, sustainable development, and the protection of our shared ocean.

Our progress was always defined by our willingness to engage, adapt, and contribute.

Our experience has taught us an important lesson.

Vulnerability does not diminish our capacity to make a difference.

If anything, it gives us a deeper understanding of the challenges facing the world.

As a Small Island Developing State, we understand adaptation because we live with its realities.

We understand sustainability because our future depends on it.

We understand cooperation because no nation can meet today’s challenges alone.

Especially a small one.

The question before us is not whether a small state can contribute.

The question is how we can contribute more.

Today, the world faces challenges that do not recognise borders.

Climate change is accelerating.

Economic uncertainty is affecting communities everywhere.

Geopolitical tensions are placing greater pressure on the international system.

In this environment, cooperation is the foundation upon which our shared future depends.

The Maldives will continue to support an open, rules-based international order where all states have their sovereignty respected, their voices heard, and their interests protected.

We stand for dialogue, and diplomacy.

We support multilateralism and international cooperation.

These are the fundamentals of President Dr Muizzu’s Maldives First Foreign Policy

Protecting our interests, while contributing to make the world better.

Making our voices heard, especially on issues near and dear to us.

This is why we are seeking membership of the Human Rights Council for the term 2028-2030.

And why we will be a member of the Economic and Social Council for the term 2027-2029.

This is why we are seeking membership of the Security Council for the term 2033-2034.

This is why we are seeking to host Conferences, workshops, and seminars here in the Maldives.

Including the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in 2028.

Because we do not believe – for one second – that size determines destiny.

Our shores remain open for friends who respect us, for partners who value us, and for investments that nourish us.

As we celebrate our independence, we also renew our invitation to our friends and partners.

Come and experience the warmth of the Maldives and the hospitality of our people.

Come and explore opportunities to invest, innovate, and build with us.

Come and be part of a future shaped by partnership, resilience, and shared ambition.

It’s only been a few months since I have taken on this role of Minister.

If you ask me what it is like on any given day: The answer is actually quite simple.

If the phone does not ring, you start wondering what's wrong.

If it does ring, you wonder what is wrong.

But jokes aside, I want to take a moment to say thank you.

People often see the pictures. They hear the speeches. They read the press releases.

These make the headlines.

What they don’t always see are the conversations that happen before the meeting.

The calls made across time zones.

The relationships built over years.

The trust that is earned long before agreements are signed or announcements are made.

That is the true work of diplomacy.

And it is work that none of us do alone.

And for that, once again, I thank you for your friendship and your partnership.

You have certainly made my job easier, and far more meaningful.

Sixty-one years ago, the Maldives asked the world to recognise a new nation.

Today, we stand as a partner ready to cooperate, contribute, and build together.

We remember those who believed in us at the beginning.

We value those who stand with us today.

And we welcome those who will shape the future with us tomorrow.

Because the story of the Maldives has always been built through partnership.

And the next chapter will be no different.

I also wish to thank my team – Team Khaarijee – for their team spirit, professionalism, and their excellent work.

I thank you.

en.title: Statement by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, at the World Environment Day Tree Planting Initiative Central Park, Hulhumalé
en.description: Minister of Climate Change, Environment and Energy His Excellency Ali Shareef,
en.body:
Minister of Climate Change, Environment and Energy His Excellency Ali Shareef,

Managing Director of Housing Development Cooperation Brigadier General (Retired) Ali Zuhair,

Ambassadors, High Commissioners, distinguished guests, and dear colleagues,

Assalamalaikum and a very good evening to you all.

It is a pleasure to welcome you here today as we come together to mark World Environment Day through this tree planting initiative.

We gather here, around a simple but powerful idea.

Sixty trees for sixty years.

The significance of this initiative lies in what it represents.

This year, the Maldives is marking sixty years of its independence.

Over six decades, we have moved…

…from the foundations of statehood to the strengthening of our democratic institutions
…from defining our identity to establishing our place in the international community.

It has been a journey of nation-building, adaptation, and resilience.

That work continues today as we confront new challenges built on the progress we have achieved.

It is therefore fitting that we mark this milestone through an environmental initiative.

Our story on the international stage is inseparable from the environment itself.

We are a nation whose voice is both respected and heard in global discussions on climate change, environmental protection, and sustainable development.

Successive generations of leaders and diplomats have worked to ensure that the concerns of Small Island Developing States are reflected in international decision-making.

For the Maldives, protecting the environment means protecting our people, livelihoods, economy, and culture.

Climate change is our present reality. Rising sea levels, coastal erosion, shifting weather patterns, and growing pressure on fragile ecosystems underscore the urgency of climate action.

While global cooperation remains essential, resilience must also be built at home through sustained effort and shared responsibility.

It must be across our society.

Environmental advocacy is more than international agreements alone.

It must also be reflected in the choices we make, as governments, as institutions, as communities, and as individuals.

This event reflects the vision of His Excellency President Dr Mohamed Muizzu, who has placed sustainability at the centre of national development, with a focus on building greener, healthier and resilient communities.

The President’s 5 million trees-planting initiative is guided by the principle that sustainability is a shared responsibility : demanding the active partnership of the government, the private sector, civil society, and individual citizens alike.

And it is through this shared effort that climate resilience is built.

Today's initiative reflects that vision in action.

And, there is perhaps no better setting for this initiative than Hulhumalé.

The diplomatic enclave that is being developed in Hulhumalé, will become our home.

For many members of the diplomatic community, Hulhumalé is infact already home. And for many of our staff too.

It is where your families are raised, your children grow, and where an important part of our national future is being written.

Every plant we place in the ground today represents an investment in that future.

It will contribute to making Hulhumalé greener, healthier, and more resilient. And in turn, our country more sustainable, and resilient.

As we mark World Environment Day and sixty years of independence, we turn our focus to the future.

The choices we make today will shape what the next generation inherits.

Let the sixty trees we plant together stand as living symbols of what we build, and what we choose to preserve.

I take this opportunity to thank the Ministry of Climate Change, Environment and Energy, especially the Five Million Tree Programme Unit, the Housing Development Corporation, the Ministry staff, and all those who contributed to making this initiative possible.

I also thank the diplomatic community present here today.

Together, you have helped turn this initiative into a meaningful expression of our collective responsibility to the environment and to the generations that will follow.

I thank you.

en.title: Her Excellency Ms.Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, at the 7th China-South Asia Cooperation Forum
en.description: Excellencies, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen,
en.body:
Excellencies, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Good afternoon, and Assalaamu Alaikum.

We meet at a time of profound global transformation. Geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, climate-related challenges, and growing pressures on multilateral institutions continue to reshape the international landscape.

In our interconnected world, events in one region can have implications well beyond their borders. This makes collaboration and mutual engagement more important than ever.

Against this backdrop, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East highlights the enduring importance of dialogue and diplomacy in safeguarding international peace and security. Beyond its humanitarian impact, the conflict has had significant repercussions for global stability and prosperity, while raising concerns about the capacity of the international system to respond collectively to emerging challenges.

For small island developing states such as the Maldives, the effects of such crises are often amplified, highlighting our vulnerability to external developments and the importance of a peaceful and stable international environment.

In the face of ongoing crises, collective action remains indispensable. No nation can address the complex challenges of our time alone. Our ability to build a more peaceful and secure world depends on learning the lessons of the past and having the courage to take affirmative action. Meeting these challenges will require unity and resolve, guided by a shared sense of purpose.

It is for these reasons that the Maldives chose to participate in this Forum. China has consistently emphasized consensus, common prosperity, and cooperative approaches to global challenges. These principles continue to resonate across our region, reflecting our aspirations for development and stronger regional ties.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

China, and in particular Yunnan Province, has been a valued partner in the Maldives' development journey. Our friendship, forged across mountains and seas, is built on mutual respect, enduring goodwill, and a shared commitment to improving the lives of our peoples.

Anchored by these principles, and by the Maldives' steadfast commitment to the One-China Principle, our bilateral relationship continues to flourish.

Over the years, cooperation across a wide range of economic and development sectors, supported by the Free Trade Agreement, has deepened the close partnership between our two countries. Today, China is one of the Maldives' largest trading partners and its largest source market for tourism.

Landmark projects such as the China-Maldives Friendship Bridge have had a transformative impact on the Maldives, strengthening national connectivity. Today, the bridge stands as a lasting symbol of the friendship between our two countries and the tangible benefits of our cooperation.

President Dr Mohamed Muizzu’s State Visit to China in 2024 and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Summit in Tianjin in 2025 marked a new chapter in Maldives–China relations, culminating in the establishment of a Comprehensive Strategic Cooperative Partnership.

Building on this foundation, we look forward to expanding cooperation, including through China’s four global initiatives, in ways that contribute to our national development priorities.

Yunnan Province, with its rich history as a gateway for cultural exchange and regional connectivity, embodies the spirit of openness and cooperation that this Forum seeks to promote.

While this is my first visit to Kunming, I had the pleasure of visiting China in 2017, and continue to carry fond memories of the warmth, hospitality, and friendship extended to me during that visit. Those memories serve as a personal reminder of the close bonds between our peoples and the enduring partnership between the Maldives and China.

As I conclude, I wish to express my sincere appreciation to the Governor of Yunnan Province, His Excellency Wang Yubo, the Organizing Committee, and the Government of the People's Republic of China for their warm welcome and hospitality, and for convening this important Forum—a valuable platform for meaningful dialogue and stronger regional cooperation.

Looking ahead, the Maldives guided by President Dr. Muizzu’s Maldives first foreign policy, remains committed to working closely with China and all our partners to strengthen ties and deepen mutual understanding. We look forward to building on the Comprehensive Strategic Cooperative Partnership and advancing our vision of a Maldives–China community with a shared future.
Ultimately, the strength of any relationship lies not only in shared interests, but in the trust, understanding, and goodwill that sustain it—values that will continue to guide relations between our two countries in the years ahead.

Thank you.

en.title: Keynote Address by Her Excellency Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, at the Opening Ceremony of the Asia World Model United Nations XIV Kurumba Maldives, Maldives
en.description: Minister of Education, Higher Education and Skills Development His Excellency Dr Ismail Shafeeu,
en.body:
Minister of Education, Higher Education and Skills Development His Excellency Dr Ismail Shafeeu,

President of International Global Network Muhammad Fahrizal,

Distinguished guests, teachers, students and visiting delegates,

Assalamalaikum and a very good morning to you all.

It is a pleasure to join you here at the opening of the fourteenth iteration of the Asia World Model United Nations.

If you have ever opened Instagram or Tiktok for a “quick” scroll you will be very familiar with this pattern.

One moment it is a meme. The next, a promo we skip. Then, suddenly a flood. Then, a conflict. And then a protest in a place you just learnt of.

Everything appears in the same feed at the same speed.

That, in itself, says something important about the world we live in today.

What is far away, and what is right in front of you, are no longer separated.

And your generation understands this better than any generation before it.

And that is both a privilege and a responsibility.

A privilege because you are more connected, informed and aware.

A responsibility because the pace makes it harder to understand, reflect and respond meaningfully.

Today, we are living through a period of profound uncertainty.

Climate change is placing pressure on vulnerable communities.

Public health systems are continuing to face stress and inequality.

Political polarisation, misinformation and distrust are weakening cohesion within societies, and cooperation between nations.

These are not isolated issues.

They are interconnected challenges in an interconnected world.

They remind us of the simple - but important truth, that no one country, one institution, or one leader alone can solve those uncertainties. Address those challenges.

In a world shaped by interdependence, progress must depend on engagement. It must depend on rules, partnerships, and mutual respect.

This is a principle that small states like the Maldives have long understood.

Sixty years ago, the Maldives chose precisely that path.

When we were admitted as the 117th Member State of the United Nations, we were a newly independent nation with limited resources and an uncertain future.

Back then, many questioned whether a Small Island Developing State (SIDS) could ever have a meaningful voice in shaping global affairs.

They questioned whether we could fully undertake the responsibilities of being a member of the global community.

But the Maldives understood an important reality from the very beginning: in a system defined by interdependence, size does not determine relevance. Engagement does.

And so, we chose not to stand at the margins but to participate in it.

We learned to navigate its structures. We contributed within its institutions. And over time, we helped shape parts of it.

For the Maldives, multilateralism has been essential. It has been the space through which a small state likes us ensures that its concerns are heard and prioritised.

We are proud to be a strong advocate for climate action, sustainable development, and the protection of human rights.

We have worked to ensure that the realities of SIDS are tests of the international system’s credibility.

Outdated global financial architectures, persistent inequality, financing gaps, and the widening digital divide continue to constrain progress.

This is why the Maldives continues to support a United Nations that is stronger, more representative, and more responsive.

This is why responsibility must be shared.

And why leadership today must be responsible.

Choosing between clear right and wrong is, in many ways, the easier part.

The harder task is making decisions between imperfect outcomes.

It requires judgement. It requires restraint. And it requires a clear sense of purpose.

Because in the end, cooperation matters. Trust matters. And, dialogue matters.

These are habits that must be cultivated early. In classrooms. In conversations. And, in debates such as the ones you will engage during this conference.

This is where platforms like Model United Nations play an important role.

At one level, it is a simulation of diplomacy. But its real value lies elsewhere.

It also teaches something that is rare.

The ability to listen to those you disagree with, without dismissing them.

It teaches patience. Discipline. Empathy.

And to defend principles while still respecting differences.

These are not just conference skills.

These are survival skills for the 21st century.

So do not underestimate your role here.

Age is not the determinant of relevance.

Engagement is. Curiosity is. And the willingness to learn is.

We are living in a time where every crisis is visible in real time.

In such an environment, the challenge is perspective.

The question before you is, not whether you will shape the future.

You will.

The question is what kind of future you will help to shape.

One that is more divided, or more cooperative,
… more cynical, or more constructive,
… more unstable, or more resilient.

Despite the uncertainty around us, I remain optimistic.

Not because the challenges are small.

But because I believe in the capacity of people, especially young people like you, to rise to meet them.

The tides of tomorrow are not fixed.

They will be shaped by the values you uphold, the choices you make, and the courage you demonstrate when faced with difficult decisions.

So participate fully in this conference.

Speak with confidence.

Listen with humility.

Lead with integrity.

And remember that the future is something you help create.

I wish all of you a meaningful conference, thoughtful discussions, lasting friendships, and an inspiring journey ahead.

I thank you.

en.title: Remarks by His Excellency Dr. Abdulla Khaleel, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, at the Extraordinary Open-Ended Meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation Executive Committee
en.description: Minister for Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Gambians Abroad of the Republic of The Gambia, His Excellency Sering Modou Njie,
en.body:
Minister for Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Gambians Abroad of the Republic of The Gambia, His Excellency Sering Modou Njie,

Minister of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates of the State of Palestine, Her Excellency Dr. Varsen Aghabekian Shahuin,

Secretary General of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, His Excellency Hissein Brahim Taha,

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Assalamu Alaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakatuhu,

We meet again at a critical moment. Since we last met, almost a year ago in this very hall, we unfortunately find ourselves discussing once again the fate of our Palestinian brothers and sisters.

During this holy month of Ramadan, we are reminded of compassion, justice, and moral responsibility. Yet even during this sacred time, Palestinians continue to endure occupation and dispossession.

While we fast and pray, their land is being confiscated in the occupied West Bank under the label of “state property.”

This decision by Israel seeks to impose an illegal reality on the ground. It expands settlements and deepens the process of annexation.

These actions clearly violate international law. They undermine prospects for peace and deny the Palestinian people their fundamental rights.

Excellencies,

Let us be clear: Palestinian lands belong to Palestinians.

For decades, we have witnessed the steady expansion of settlements across the occupied West Bank. Homes have been demolished, communities displaced, and Palestinian families stripped of their rights. Each new announcement of settlement expansion or land appropriation tightens the grip of occupation and pushes the prospects of peace further out of reach.

The Maldives strongly condemns the Israeli occupation’s decision to convert land into so-called ‘state property.’ This constitutes a serious violation of international law and represents a continuation of illegal settlement policies that undermine the rights of the Palestinian people.

Excellencies,

The only lasting resolution can be achieved through the establishment of an independent and sovereign State of Palestine, based on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

In line with our principled position, the Maldives is doing all it can:

At the International Court of Justice

At the United Nations

At home, through punitive measures

By supporting humanitarian efforts, including UNRWA

And by always lending our voice, our solidarity, our support.

Excellencies,

The Palestinian people have endured decades of occupation and denial of their fundamental rights, yet their resilience remains unbroken. Their right to self-determination is non-negotiable and their homeland is not for sale.

We need to think together, look within ourselves – at what it is that we, as a collective ummah can do. Not just words, but concrete actions.

The Maldives will not waver in its support. We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people – to freedom, to sovereignty, and to living in dignity, peace, and security on their own land.

I thank you.

en.title: Remarks by His Excellency Dr. Abdulla Khaleel Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives at the General Debate of the 61st Session of the Human Rights Council
en.description: Mr. President,
en.body:
Mr. President,

Mr. High Commissioner,

Excellencies, Ladies, and Gentlemen.

It is an honour to address this Council for a second time.

When the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in December 1948, it did more than articulate ideals. It distilled centuries of human struggle into a simple principle that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

Since then, the international community has built a remarkable legal architecture to protect that principle. Treaties were written. Institutions were created. Norms were agreed upon. And together, they form one of humanity’s most ambitious undertakings.

But progress does not move in a straight line.

The complexities of the modern world test not only our institutions, but our convictions. They compel us to ask whether the promises we made to one another and to future generations, are strong enough to withstand the pressures of rapid change, deepening inequality, and growing uncertainty.

For the Maldives, this much is clear.

The challenges may be new. The pace may be faster. The tools may be different. But the values upon which our success depends on are not. And it is through multilateralism that those values find meaning and purpose.

The Maldives is committed to the promotion and protection of human rights, both domestically and internationally. For us, it is an essential foundation for sustainable and inclusive development.

Domestically, we continue to strengthen democratic governance, the rule of law, and institutional accountability. Since the adoption of our 2008 Constitution, our democratic institutions have steadily matured through successive electoral cycles, with Presidential and Parliamentary elections widely recognised by international and domestic observers as peaceful, inclusive, and credible. Alongside this consolidation, broad legislative and institutional reforms have been undertaken to reinforce governance, combat corruption, expand labour protections, and strengthen access to justice.

These reforms include measures to enhance accountability within law enforcement and the justice sector, strengthen oversight mechanisms, and promote a rights-centred approach to public administration. Institutional capacity has been reinforced through legislative reform, professional training, and improved safeguards to ensure transparency, due process, and public trust.

We have prioritised inclusion and social equity. Women’s participation in local governance has increased substantially through electoral quotas, while targeted financial schemes support women entrepreneurs, including women with disabilities. National action plans guide reforms to advance the rights of persons with disabilities, strengthen child protection systems, and expand access to social services. Targeted programmes are being conducted for young people. We are expanding access to education, healthcare, and social welfare. These measures reflect our commitment to building an inclusive society grounded in dignity, opportunity, and equal protection under the law.

Internationally, the Maldives engages with the human rights system in the same constructive spirit. We recently concluded our fourth cycle of the Universal Periodic Review and continue active engagement with treaty bodies. We also maintain a standing invitation to all Special Procedures Mandate Holders and value their recommendations as an important contribution to our ongoing reform efforts.

Mr. President,

As a Small Island Developing State, the Maldives has consistently sought to champion an inclusive approach to human rights. One that recognises the particular challenges faced by Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States, and the importance of ensuring their meaningful and sustained participation in this Council. This conviction has guided our support for initiatives that address capacity constraints and enable LDCs and SIDS to engage fully and constructively in the Council’s work.

We have consistently called for accountability for human rights violations. Especially in Palestine, where Israel has repeatedly violated international law, threatened regional stability, destroyed civilian infrastructure, and undermined genuine hope for peace and progress. Despite repeated violations of international law, Israel continues to receive preferential trade treatment and arms transfers that fuel further aggression against the Palestinian people. We reaffirm our steadfast support for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination, and for an independent, sovereign State of Palestine established on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. The State of Palestine must be admitted as a full member of the United Nations.

We believe that the integrity of the multilateral system depends on the collective commitment of all States – small and large - to uphold justice, inclusivity, and peace through the universal respect for human rights, without selectivity or exception.

Our most recent term on this Council, which concluded last year, reaffirmed our belief in the power of constructive engagement. Building on that experience, and guided by our continued commitment to universality, inclusion, dialogue and cooperation, the Maldives will be seeking election to the Human Rights Council for the term 2028-2030. We seek your support in these elections.

Mr. President,

As the international human rights landscape continues to evolve, this Council has a central responsibility to ensure that the system it stewards remains credible in its standards, inclusive in its processes, and effective in its impact.

The Maldives will continue to engage constructively and in good faith, working closely with the Office of the High Commissioner, Member States, and civil society, to strengthen implementation and cooperation where it matters most.

In doing so, we remain guided by the promise of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; that human rights are universal, indivisible and inseparable from human dignity.

I thank you.

en.title: Statement by His Excellency Dr Abdulla Khaleel Minister of for Foreign Affairs at United Nations Alliance of Civilizations Group of Friends High-level Meeting
en.description: Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm. His Highness Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,
en.body:
Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm.

His Highness Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,

Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

It is often said that small islands read the world differently.

We live close to the horizon, where every shift in tide or wind is felt immediately.

Perhaps for that reason, the Maldives has long treated dialogue not as diplomatic ritual but as a form of resilience, a way to remain steady in a world that rarely slows down for anyone.

In an era where divisions deepen both offline and online, UNAOC’s work is a safeguard against fragmentation. By anticipating emerging challenges such as climate-induced displacement and digital misinformation, it ensures that dialogue remains a force for unity and human dignity.

As UNAOC marks its twentieth anniversary, its enduring mission reminds us that building bridges between cultures is not a choice but a responsibility we share for a more peaceful and inclusive world.

Excellencies,

Dialogue is how we make sense of uncertainty; it is how we negotiate co-existence, and it is how we build trust in a world that is not always inclined towards us.

For countries like mine, dialogue is a necessity that shapes our security, our identity and our relationship far beyond our shores.

The Maldives does not come to admit the architecture of dialogue; we come to test its strength.

We come to ask whether our collective commitment to understanding is strong enough for a world in which division spreads faster than reason, and in which narratives harden long before facts are established.

A multipolar world is often described in terms of shifting power centres. But its deeper implications are cultural.

Polarisation is no longer confined to politics; it permeates the social and informational spaces people inhabit.

It shapes how communities interpret one another and how they interpret themselves.

Dialogue cannot afford to be decorative. It must help rebuild trust that has eroded across communities and countries.

Excellencies,

For the Maldives, this mission is inseparable from the environment that shapes our existence.

Long before climate change became a defining global issue, island societies understood that the stability of the natural world underpins the stability of the social world. When the environment fractures, cohesion fractures.

Today, rising seas threaten not only our physical territory but our cultural inheritance, our language, our traditions, our sense of continuity.

Cooperation is no longer optional; it is a matter of cultural survival. Any global commitment to respect among civilizations must include respect for the right of vulnerable nations to endure.

We face another form of fragility: the volatility of the digital sphere.

The new frontier of misunderstanding is not at borders but on screens. Hostility can be manufactured, identities distorted, and young people exposed to manipulation before they have the tools to recognize it.

What once took years to divide societies can now happen in days, leaving consequences that endure for generations.

As the UNAOC enters its next chapter, the Maldives believes our task is not only to respond to emerging divides, but to anticipate them. The world ahead will test our collective capacity for empathy, restraint, and imagination.

If we invest now in dialogue that is practical, inclusive, and grounded in human dignity, we can shape a future in which diversity is a source of stability rather than tension.

I thank you.

en.title: Remarks by His Excellency Dr. Abdulla Khaleel, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives, at the Roundtable on Upholding International Justice Systems and the Rule of Law session held at the 23rd Doha Forum
en.description: Thank you, Moderator. It is a pleasure to join this important roundtable.
en.body:
Thank you, Moderator. It is a pleasure to join this important roundtable.

As we meet for the 23rd edition of the Doha Forum held under the patronage of His Highness the Amir, we are reminded of Qatar’s steadfast commitment to dialogue diplomacy, and the strengthening of multilateral cooperation.

This year’s theme, “Justice in Action: Beyond Promises to Progress,” is both timely and pivotal. Around the world, we see widening inequalities, prolonged conflicts, and deepening humanitarian crises amidst changing geopolitical dynamics. These realities demand not only our attention, but mandates us to renew the commitment to uphold international justice and the rule of law – precisely, the foundation of global stability.

For the Maldives — as a small island developing State — a functioning, fair, and impartial international justice system is not a luxury. It is essential. Our security, our sovereignty, and our ability to thrive depend on a rules-based international order where all States are equal, where international law is consistently applied, and where justice cannot be shaped by power or political convenience.

In this context, it is important to recognise that climate justice is a core part of international justice. For small island countries like the Maldives and many other
like- minded states, climate change has increasingly become an existential threat. Those of us who contribute the least to climate change are often the ones who suffer the most. How the global community addresses climate impacts, loss and damage, and environmental vulnerability are real tests of whether the global justice system is fair. A truly fair international system must reflect this and include climate justice as a central aspect of global accountability.

Yet today, confidence in our international justice system remains fragile amid growing global pressures. We are concerned about selectivity, delays, and uneven enforcement of international law. This has contributed to erosion of trust and weakened the legitimacy of multilateral mechanisms designed to protect human dignity.  We must act decisively to reinforce and uphold these institutions, to restore faith and ensure justice for all.

Excellencies,

Ensuring that international courts and mechanisms can function with full independence and credibility is a shared responsibility. The International Court of Justice (ICJ), in particular, should be able to play its full role in guiding peaceful dispute resolution and upholding the rule of law. For countries like the Maldives, the ICJ represents fairness and predictability, a place where disputes can be settled through principles, not power. Supporting its work, and respecting its decisions, is essential to maintaining confidence in the multilateral system.

The Maldives has consistently demonstrated principled leadership in advocating for accountability within ICJ processes through our support for cases that uphold human rights and protect vulnerable communities. Our engagement reflects our belief that even small states can meaningfully contribute to strengthening global justice

Justice must also contribute to peace. Transitional justice must be inclusive, community-centred, and focused on reconciliation.

Above all, justice must protect human dignity, anywhere and everywhere. Whether in Gaza, Sudan, or any region in crisis, the protection of civilians and respect for humanitarian law must remain universal obligations. These principles cannot depend on geography or politics.

For the Maldives, the plight of the Palestinian people remains a profound test of our shared commitment to justice. We have consistently advocated for accountability, for the protection of innocent civilians in Palestine, and for an end to the atrocities and violence that has claimed far too many innocent lives. We firmly believe that international law must guide the path to a just and lasting peace, one that ensures the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination and statehood. Justice delayed in Palestine is justice denied on a global scale.

Likewise, the suffering of the Rohingya community stands as a stark reminder of the human cost of inaction. The Maldives has taken a principled stand in support of accountability for the atrocities faced by the Rohingya including through international legal proceedings in the ICJ. As a nation with deep belief in the rule of law, we cannot remain indifferent when an entire population is denied basic human rights and forced into displacement. Their plight underscores why international justice must be accessible to all, especially the most marginalised.

The Maldives remains firmly committed to a rule-based international order, to multilateral cooperation, and to global justice that protects the weak and restrains the powerful. We believe that international justice is strongest when it is universal, impartial, and accessible — and when it restores hope to those who have suffered the most.

Excellencies,

Strengthening trust in the international justice system requires meaningful reforms, the depoliticisation of justice mechanisms, greater representation and participation of small states and stronger compliance and enforcement frameworks that ensure decisions are respected. These steps are essential to reinforcing the legitimacy and credibility of international justice

At the end of the day, justice is not delivered through declarations. It is realised through action, through empathy, and through a renewed commitment to our shared humanity. Let us use this Forum to renew our collective resolve to uphold justice, strengthen institutions, and deliver outcomes that advance human dignity and lasting peace for all peoples.

Thank you.

en.title: Statement by His Excellency Dr Abdulla Khaleel, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Maldives at the General Debate of the Eightieth Session of the United Nations General Assembly
en.description: بســم اللّـه الرّحمـن الرّحيــم
en.body:
بســم اللّـه الرّحمـن الرّحيــم

Madam President,
Mr Secretary-General,
Excellencies,
Ladies and Gentlemen.

On the twenty-first of this month, we marked the sixtieth anniversary of the Maldives joining the United Nations.

Over the last sixty years, we have placed our confidence in this institution and in the multilateral system it represents: a promise that sovereignty matters, borders are respected, and every country—small or large—has an equal voice in shaping our shared future.

That confidence was never naïve.
It rested on the conviction that laws restrain might, and rules hold firm against coercion.

But assurances endure only when the rules-based order is upheld.
When it is breached without accountability, we lose more than order; we lose faith in the system itself.
And when faith collapses, it is not peace that fills the void.
It is unrestrained might: power that redraws boundaries, silences voices, and tramples norms.

This is the erosion we confront — three fault-lines in the global order.

First, the taboo against conquest.
For many decades, the rule that borders cannot be changed by force underwrote peace.
That foundation is cracking.
Every breach, once allowed, becomes precedent.
And precedent invites repetition.

Second, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity.
These are not slogans, but the ground rules for peace, development, and dignity.
But today, powerful aggressors treat them as optional.

Third, multilateralism—the doctrine that shared challenges require shared solutions.
That doctrine is under siege.
When institutions are bypassed, when vetoes paralyze, when laws are applied selectively, confidence unravels—and with it, the system itself.

We see this erosion everywhere.

In Palestine—especially Gaza—Israel’s ongoing genocide has killed more than 66,000
civilians—more than a half of that: women and children.

In the West Bank, settler violence intensifies – trying to force more Palestinians out, and annex more land.

Israel has wilfully, shamelessly, and repeatedly, violated international law.
It has defied hundreds of resolutions of the Security Council and this Assembly.
It has rejected the decisions of the International Court of Justice and sanctioned the International Criminal Court.

People killed while begging for food.
Mothers holding lifeless babies.
Children staring blankly at the ruins of their homes and their futures.

These are the images that you simply cannot forget and move past.

And the sheer hypocrisy is…

This genocide is sustained by weapons and money from the very countries that claim to defend human rights—the same countries that helped define the very norms and laws being broken.
By their actions, they refuse to see Palestinians as equal human beings, deserving of life, dignity, and freedom.

This complicity is the shame of the century.
Let me be clear.
Famine can never be a weapon of war.
Innocents must not be mercilessly maimed, arbitrarily jailed, and ruthlessly killed.
The assault on sovereignty is equally clear in Israel’s recent illegal attacks against Qatar, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen, Tunisia, and Iran.
Each strike is a reminder that borders are trampled when power speaks louder than law.

In each case,
Where laws and norms give way to leverage;
Where responsibility gives way to convenience:
The pattern is the same.

If this erosion continues, the question will no longer be whether it will happen again, but who will be the next victim.

UN80 must be the repair moment—the turning point.

Reform is no longer optional; it is the only path forward.
Any serious reform must tackle the Security Council’s paralysis.
We need an expanded and more representative Council.
A rotating seat for SIDS is where we must start.
We need a Council that is transparent in its deliberations and accountable in its decisions to the membership and to itself.
We need a Council that does not hide under the threat of veto.

The Secretary-General’s three-track reform should be Member State–led, Member-State driven, and implementation-focused.

It should enhance the UN’s presence – especially in SIDS.
It should align mandates and secure predictable development finance.
It should ensure sufficient programme delivery staff.
“Realignment” must not mean less, but better service and better support.

We must also confront another imbalance.
The United Nations should exemplify equality.
But the shameful reality is that it has never had a female Secretary-General. The time has come to correct that.

Reform is not only about structures; it is about credibility.
And credibility lives or dies with trust in multilateralism.
